newsitem.title: MALDIVES: FEATURE-Friendly sharks roam waters of the Maldives.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Friendly sharks roam waters of the Maldives.

text.p: Sharks lurk in the warm waters around the Maldive Islands, but locals say visitors to this Indian Ocean paradise have little to fear.
For local divers, hand-feeding the sharks is fun, although the Maldivian authorities and holiday resort owners discourage the practice for fear of attracting negative publicity.
"It's not just the people of the Maldives, even the sharks are friendly here," one diver, Muhamad Hassan, says with pride.
"Our sharks are quite well-fed and not dangerous," he adds. "In fact, there have never been any incidents with sharks."
Indeed, the sharks have become something of a tourist attraction in the Maldives.

Tucked 480 km (300 miles) southwest of the southern tip of India and 720 km (450 miles) west of Sri Lanka, the Maldives is a string of about 1,200 low-lying coral islands scattered across the equator in the vast expanse of the Indian Ocean.
Tourism is central to the prosperity of the archipelago's tiny population of 250,000 Sunni Moslems.
"Twenty percent of gross domestic product, 40 percent of the government budget and 70 percent of total foreign exchange comes from tourism," Tourism Minister Ibrahim Zaki told Reuters.

Seventy four islands, with their coconut palms, white sandy beaches and fish-filled lagoons, have been developed as resorts, each run by a single company and offering water sports such as scuba diving, snorkelling, para-sailing, sailing and canoeing.
Mohamed Waseem is general manager of Kanifinolha resort on Kani island, just 178 metres (yards) long and 84 metres wide and about 30 minutes by speedboat from Male international airport.
He said 90 percent of his guests were European, mostly German and British, and 10 percent were from Asia.
Zaki said the government planned to develop new resorts to accommodate rising demand under a 10-year tourism master plan, which will increase hotel capacity by 10,000 beds.
"At the moment we have 74 resort islands with a total bed capacity of 12,500, and the first phase of the new plan, which has already started, will add 3,100 more beds," he said.
But tourism development is not simple, Zaki said.
"The biggest challenge we face in tourism is human resource availability. We have 250,000 people, but last year alone we attracted 340,000 tourists," he said.
More than half of the islanders are of school age, forcing the Maldives to allow foreigners to join the workforce.

"I would imagine 65 percent of the population is under 25 years of age," Zaki said. "Already 38 percent of the workforce in the tourism industry are expatriates from Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, the Philippines and some European countries."
While Maldivian authorities are reluctant to discuss openly the social impact of tourism on their youthful population, the traditional island lifestyle is clearly under pressure.
"We are not allowed to visit the resorts, drink alcohol or party," complained one young man, who asked not to be named. "Are they trying to isolate us from all that is around us?"
Zaki said he did not foresee a major conflict arising from the stark contrast between the freewheeling habits of Western tourists and the conservative lifestyle of the Moslem islanders.

"There is minimum contact between the local population and the tourists," he said. "This works well for both sides. The visiting tourists want privacy. To our advantage, there is minimum effect on our socio-economic life."
Tourists keen on mixing with the locals may have better luck meeting the sharks.
Diver Muhamad Hasan said some diving schools at the island resorts once held shark circuses in which divers could offer food to sharks, but have since altered their practice.
"Instead there are diving safaris in which divers are shown (with) sharks swimming close by," he said. "These are exhilarating moments, these are memorable moments."
Mohamed Waseem of Kanifinolha resort said divers are taken to special reefs in the area where they can see sharks and plenty of tropical fish.
And just why are the sharks so friendly?
"Spear-fishing is prohibited in the Maldives, so the fish are friendly and totally unafraid of divers," Mohamed Waseem explained.
